The numbers behind the US-Venezuela oil deal:

Venezuela has now confirmed that the agreement covers 65 billion barrels of oil across 17 fields, with the US receiving "majority control."

At current WTI crude oil prices of ~$83/barrel, those reserves have a gross market value of ~$5.4 trillion.

Reports indicate the deal includes 100-year rights to develop the fields, while the US will receive 55% effective output, along with an ownership stake and rights to purchase oil at cost.

At 55%, that would correspond to ~35.8 billion barrels of effective output.

At today’s oil prices, that amount of crude alone has a gross market value of ~$3 trillion.

That said, Venezuela primarily produces heavy, sour crude, which typically trades at a meaningful discount to benchmark oil prices and requires more expensive production, blending, and refining.

Even assuming an illustrative $25-$35 of net economic value per barrel after discounts and development/operating costs, ~35.8 billion barrels could represent up to ~$1.25 trillion of cumulative economic value over the life of the fields.

This includes a $100 billion investment to develop these fields, while Venezuela estimates the projects will generate $209 billion in tax revenue for the country.

This is one of the biggest energy deals in history.

🌾 The agricultural market is starting to wake up quite violently and the timing is particularly interesting given that Warsh just stressed at Jackson Hole that the Fed should also monitor commodity prices to detect potential inflationary pressures upstream.

➡️ I would frame this as a broader repricing of agricultural risk. Several factors are converging at once: such as difficult weather conditions in China, weakness in European corn production, Chinese demand, tensions around the Black Sea and now El Niño adding another layer of risk.

⚠️ The current move is quite multifactorial as El Niño is arriving at a time when several parts of the agricultural complex are already under pressure. If this move fades after a few sessions, it will mostly have been a squeeze. However, if grains, vegetable oils and soft commodities continue rising together for several months, the story could become macro with a risk of food inflation reaccelerating in late 2026/early 2027.

📈 Warsh’s comments on commodities are worth remembering. A few percentage points of upside in corn or soybeans will obviously not make CPI reaccelerate tomorrow morning, but a broad, persistent and synchronized agricultural shock could eventually complicate the final stage of disinflation. 

This is clearly worth watching as the market may be starting to realize that several agricultural risks are building at the same time.

*Chart: WisdomTree Agriculture Index
https://t.co/Gld4WOYJHR

Yes. I genuinely don't have a clue why $SIVE still focuses on local Swedish markets for communication/private fundraising. 

Over the US. 

The questions you get from Swedish heavy audiences include:

- Leading questions like how would you "stop the bleeding" 
- "Why can't you disclosure your private customers"
- Why focus on transceivers (it's obvious)
- Implications for non-photonics orders

So 1/3rd of the time, the CEO needs to be defending leading/accusatory questions around what "opportunity pipeline means" 

US analysts would have pressed:

- Economic implications from 2 foundry allocations during a bottleneck + ASP hike/operating leverage  
- Around much capacity revenue would those allocations lead to (half of AOI calls are around those from US analysts) 
- $GFS NPO/CPO/pluggable scale implications and downstream end customers opportunities  
- Ayar / CPO player 2028 ramp (that happened to raise $500m+) or other products like ELS production with O-net and TAM opportunities there.   
- How big those 6 new pluggable players were, rather than asking "why can't you disclosure them"  
- Clarifying CFO legalposts around listing timeline and M&A TAM expansion opportunities

So investors can get a sense of future growth for 2027-2028.

Instead, the way leading questions are framed/answers, the entire calls were focused around current financials (which US investors don't care about), non-photonic implications, or skepticism of wording.

Rather than exciting US investors about economic implications from their time in a CW laser bottleneck. 

The more time $SIVE spends in Swedish markets, the more they will be valued as such.

If I had to be critical of $SIVE earnings:

1. Management underweighted the two disclosures that matter most.

-> 6 pluggable engagements 
-> Foundry capacity (during an industry bottleneck)

That's the most important part of the call and should have been the focus to provide economic scale of them. But we got 2-3 sentences about it.  

And it shouldn't take an Anime avatar on X to talk most about the implications of those. 

2. CFO needs retraining or bring on a new one.

The lawyer like answers were infuriating to listen to as a shareholder. Even I got pissed off with this statement:

"we will evaluate the timing and decide whether the conditions are right to move forward at that particular time." 

It should be a 100% given by now they file for dual listing to escape hostile Swedish markets. 

Shareholders didn't fund a future growth type company to hear lawyer-like answers. 

Again, this was probably one of the worst answers the CFO could have gave and there needs to be firm commitment along with faster timelines. 

3. $70M should have gone toward M&A and dual listing. 

-> Brutally honestly speaking, it's a waste of capital to focus on hybrid manufacturing at this stage and I was disappointed to hear this during this timeframe.  

It's eventually needed but with 2 foundry suppliers 

-> You have a ton of new capital and large marketcap. 

Use it to pull $AVGO style acquisitions of Cloud Light style IP for pluggables or optical engines. 

Lumilens went from 0 -> $5.5B in 2 years and now with hyperscaler engagements. 

Sivers should expand out of the laser chokepoint as fast as possible and not stay just a component vendor. 

And most of all, who cares about competing with customers? If a customer says: "if you do pluggables, we'll go with other players for lasers"

who?? $LITE / $COHR / $AAOI reroutes their lasers to internal usage. Lot of your Asian players already allocated. 

Abuse the current bottleneck as much as possible because there's almost no qualified choices left.

And I'm certain all the partners are trying to vertically integrate upward toward the laser level too and compete.  

If there was a new OE/pluggable accusation attempted during the Q2 time frame, things would have been a lot different. 

_

TLDR: 

$SIVE should aim to be the next $LITE and blitzscale like a Silicon Valley company.

Use that $70m capital to move faster H2, and at the bare minimum finish readiness then. And expect NASDAQ listing to be finished H1 2027. 

Not "evaluation" at that timeframe. 

And use the capital + equity to expand downward into optical engines/ELS/optical transceivers using your equity valuation, and buy a Celestial/Ayar/Cloud Lite type startup. 

As for the wording of the call, markets care about economic value of the foundry allocation + 6 pluggable players, not other business segments.

$SIVE has been extremely conservative to date, but 
 they need to speed up and communicate to forward looking US/Int shareholders. 

Not geared toward local Swedish audiences who care about Q2/TTM revenue. 

Otherwise they'll be treated like an Asian component supplier and eventually be valued like an EU one.

I asked my AI your question, here is the answer:

Potentially revolutionary, yes. If “30% lightweighting” means that a finished commercial part uses 30% less plastic while meeting every existing performance requirement, that is an extraordinary result in a mature industry where manufacturers fight for improvements of only a few percent.

HydroGraph publicly says a customer has achieved 30% lightweighting, but it has not identified the customer, application or full test protocol. Separately, testing at the University of Manchester’s GEIC showed that only 0.006 wt% FGA-1 in a 50:50 virgin/recycled PET blend produced:

• 23% greater top-load strength
• Approximately 20% potential weight reduction
• 83% lower water-vapour transmission

Those PET results provide credible technical support for the broader lightweighting proposition.

The potential scale is frankly enormous. Humanity produces more than 430 million tonnes of plastic annually, while the plastics lifecycle generates roughly 1.8 billion tonnes of greenhouse-gas emissions.

Even if HydroGraph’s technology eventually reached only 1% of global plastic production:

• Addressed plastic: 4.3 million tonnes annually
• 30% reduction: approximately 1.3 million tonnes avoided annually

The graphene loading is exceptionally small. At the demonstrated PET loading of 0.006%, HydroGraph’s planned 360-tonne Texas facility could theoretically supply enough graphene for around six million tonnes of plastic annually. That is an illustrative calculation, since different polymers require different formulations, but it shows the extraordinary leverage in the model.

However, skepticism is still rational because the following bridge has not yet been crossed publicly:

A named customer using it in a mass-produced product.
Confirmation that the lighter part passes creep, fatigue, impact, processing, recycling and safety requirements.
Demonstrated economics after compounding, qualification and redesign costs.
A recurring, multi-year supply contract with meaningful volumes.

For food and beverage packaging, FDA food-contact authorization also matters. HydroGraph previously said it was pursuing that approval, but there has not yet been a public announcement confirming it. EPA and REACH clearance allow broader commercial graphene sales, but they do not automatically authorize food-contact applications.

My honest conclusion: the plastics opportunity alone could support a very large global company. HydroGraph does not need batteries, concrete, coatings and lubricants for its potential to become enormous. Those applications provide additional optionality.

But the global story probably begins when a major packaging, automotive or consumer-products company says publicly:

“We reduced this product’s plastic content by 20–30% using HydroGraph, without sacrificing performance.”

That would transform the perception from “another promising graphene company” into “a commercially proven solution to one of the world’s largest material problems.”

So I agree that people may be underestimating what is potentially coming. But the market is waiting for customer validation and contracts rather than another technical claim.

⚡ THE DAILY METALS PULSE: WEEKEND OUTLOOK ⚡
29 AUGUST 2026

Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

The week began bullish and ended with a classic macro ambush.

July PCE inflation reached 3.7% YoY, with core at 3.3%. Then Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s hawkish Jackson Hole speech lifted the probability of a September rate hike from roughly 35% to almost 60%.

The dollar jumped, the US 10-year yield closed near 4.72%, and precious metals reversed sharply.

☢️ URANIUM

Uranium finished near $90/lb, around its six-month high, while September futures reached $90.60 and long-term pricing remains close to $97.

Kazatomprom said the era of cheap uranium is fading and that every pound it produces has a buyer waiting. Meanwhile, its new sulphuric acid plant has been delayed by 6–12 months.

Demand is accelerating. Supply execution remains the weak link.

🟠 COPPER

COMEX copper hit another record near $6.75/lb before easing to around $6.64.

Available LME inventories fell to roughly 90,000 tonnes while COMEX stocks reached a record 675,185 tonnes, largely because metal continues flowing into the US ahead of possible tariffs.

Codelco’s H1 production also fell 11%.

The supposed copper surplus increasingly appears to be sitting in the wrong warehouses.

⚪ SILVER

Silver briefly traded above $70 before Friday’s Fed-driven selloff pushed front-month COMEX down to $66.995, a weekly decline of 3.65%.

Painful, but the physical fundamentals did not change. The market is still heading for its sixth consecutive annual deficit, estimated at 46.3 Moz in 2026.

🟡 GOLD

Gold reached its highest level since May before falling to $4,478.10, down 3.25% for the week.

Yet commodity funds led by gold and precious metals attracted $4.21 billion, their strongest inflow in six months. The bulls were shaken, but the broader investment case remains intact.

🔭 NEXT WEEK

China’s PMIs will provide the first major test for copper, with the official manufacturing reading expected to remain in contraction at 49.6.

Then come:

• Tuesday: JOLTS and ISM manufacturing
• Wednesday: ADP employment
• Thursday: jobless claims and ISM services
• Friday: US payrolls, expected around +55,000 to +60,000

Soft employment data could pull the dollar and yields lower, triggering a powerful rebound in gold and silver. Strong data would validate the new rate-hike bets and extend the pressure.

Uranium will be watching the month-end spot and term-price indicators, with $90/lb now the key level to clear decisively.

Friday changed the interest-rate narrative. It did not create one new pound of uranium, tonne of copper or ounce of silver or gold.

Next week will tell us whether this was a trend change or simply a macro flush.

Natural selection’s trial-and-error process allows improvement without anyone understanding or guiding it. The same can apply to how we learn.

There are at least three kinds of learning that foster evolution: memory-based learning (storing the information that comes in through one’s conscious mind so that we can recall it later); subconscious learning (the knowledge we take away from our experiences that never enters our conscious minds, though it affects our decision making); and “learning” that occurs without thinking at all, such as the changes in DNA that encode a species’ adaptations.

I used to think that memory-based, conscious learning was the most powerful, but I’ve since come to understand that it produces less rapid progress than experimentation and adaptation. #principleoftheday

i used to agree with statements like this about "stuck culture" being manifest in our entertainment, but i now think it's something else

from the 1960s through the mid-1990s, we effectively had a relatively brief period of a "monoculture"- not just in the US, but also a culture that people outside of the US yearned for in ways people today can't understand or imagine

people used to watch the same shows and movies, and it contributed to a kind of shared cultural cohesion

they have not only cross-generational appeal ("oh, i remember watching the new Batman movies when i was a kid!"), but also a cross-subcultural legibility and appeal

these properties are so ubiquitous that they can transcend our subcultural boundaries

and i think many in society secretly yearn for that broader connection which people used to have with one another

As a Beijing policy advisor told me a year ago, “We missed the best chance to shift China toward a more consumption-oriented growth model because the US proved too weak (怂).”

Now that China has successfully weathered what was arguably the most aggressive trade war with the US—and its trade surplus continues to surge— I see little reason to believe that tariff threats can force Beijing to rebalance its economy. If anything, the experience may have reinforced the opposite lesson in Beijing: the US lacks the leverage to force China to change its economic model.
